concepts.name: Sound
concepts.why: Sound is a disturbance of matter that is transmitted from its source outward, and it is a wave. On the atomic scale it is a disturbance of atoms that is far more ordered than their thermal motions, and in many instances it is a periodic wave in which the atoms undergo simple harmonic motion. Defining sound this way, in terms of physics rather than perception, is what lets the chapter treat ultrasound, which is never heard, with the same ideas as speech.
concepts.evidence: The section defines sound in its second paragraph and returns to the definition in its summary; the introduction's fallen tree is the case the definition settles, and the shattered glass of Figure 17.2 shows the effects of a sound that is not itself visible.

concepts.name: Sound as a longitudinal pressure wave
concepts.why: A vibrating string compresses the air in front of it and expands the air behind it, and these compressions and rarefactions move out as longitudinal pressure waves having the same frequency as the string. Sound waves in air and most fluids are longitudinal because fluids have almost no shear strength. A graph of gauge pressure against distance from the source is a sine wave, and the pressures vary only slightly from atmospheric for ordinary sounds. The amplitude decreases with distance because the energy is spread over a larger area, is absorbed by objects such as the eardrum, and is turned into thermal motion by the viscosity of air and by heat transfer between compressions and rarefactions.
concepts.evidence: Figures 17.3, 17.4 and 17.5 draw the string and the compressions leaving it, with the gauge-pressure graph in 17.5; Figure 17.6 shows the compressions travelling up the ear canal and the net force they put on the eardrum; the paragraph on the decrease of amplitude with distance names the second law of thermodynamics.

concepts.name: Hearing
concepts.why: Hearing is the perception of sound, just as vision is the perception of visible light. The physical phenomenon and its perception are related but not the same thing, and the chapter keeps them apart: wavelength, frequency, amplitude and speed of propagation belong to the wave, and pitch and loudness belong to the listener.
concepts.evidence: The section defines hearing in its first paragraph and its glossary; 17.6 restates the definition and gives each perception its physical quantity in Table 17.4.

concepts.name: Pitch
concepts.why: Perception of frequency is called pitch. You can sense the frequency of a sound directly, and the wavelength is sensed only indirectly, through the correlation of the size of a musical instrument with its pitch: small instruments such as a piccolo make high-pitch, short-wavelength sounds and large instruments such as a tuba make low-pitch, long-wavelength ones.
concepts.evidence: The first paragraph defines pitch and gives the piccolo and the tuba; the second Check Your Understanding asks how to tell a high-pitch instrument from a low-pitch one without hearing either, and 17.6 returns to pitch and to how finely it is discriminated.

concepts.name: Speed of sound, frequency and wavelength, $\kvw = \kf\klam$
concepts.why: The relationship of the speed of sound, its frequency and its wavelength is the same as for all waves. The wavelength is the distance between adjacent identical parts of the wave, for example between adjacent compressions, and the frequency is that of the source, the number of waves that pass a point per unit time. In a given medium under fixed conditions the speed is constant, so the higher the frequency, the smaller the wavelength.
concepts.evidence: The equation is stated twice and is the summary's first line; Figure 17.8 marks all three quantities on a tuning fork's wave; Example 17.1 finds the wavelengths at the two ends of the audible range; the problems on the soprano's shriek, the 0.10 m wavelength and the 1500 Hz tone each solve it for one quantity.

concepts.name: The speed of sound depends on the medium
concepts.why: The speed of sound in a medium is determined by a combination of the medium's rigidity, or compressibility in gases, and its density. The more rigid or less compressible the medium, the faster the speed of sound, and for materials of similar rigidity sound travels faster through the one with the lower density. The speed of sound in air is low because air is compressible, and it is generally greater in liquids and solids. Earthquakes show the same dependence: longitudinal P-waves outrun transverse S-waves in granite because its bulk modulus is greater than its shear modulus.
concepts.evidence: Table 17.1 lists the speed of sound in gases, liquids and solids; the earthquake paragraph applies the idea to P- and S-waves; the keyed AP item on the teacher's voice tests whether speaking underwater or raising the temperature changes the speed; the problem on the 5.96 cm wavelength at 100 kHz asks which substance of the table it is.

concepts.name: Speed of sound in air and temperature, $\kvw = (331\ \text{m/s})\sqrt{\kTemp/273\ \text{K}}$
concepts.why: For air at sea level the speed of sound is 331 m/s at 0 °C and grows as the square root of the kelvin temperature, because the speed of sound in a gas is related to the average speed of its particles, which itself goes as the square root of the temperature. The dependence is real but not strong: at 20.0 °C the speed is 343 m/s, less than a 4% increase.
concepts.evidence: The equation is stated with the rms speed beside it and repeated in the summary; Example 17.1 evaluates it at 30.0 °C; the problems on 20.0 °C air, the Sahara, the two fireworks and the bat at 5.00 °C and 35.0 °C all begin from it, and 17.5's tube problems use it to find the speed on a given day.

concepts.name: The speed of sound is nearly independent of frequency
concepts.why: In open air the speed of sound is the same for all frequencies in the audible range. If it were not, the music of a marching band would arrive out of cadence, the low-pitch instruments lagging the high-pitch ones more the farther away you stood; because all instruments arrive together at any distance, all frequencies travel at nearly the same speed, and so a fixed speed ties frequency and wavelength together.
concepts.evidence: The marching-band argument is the section's own; Figure 17.10 draws the woofer's long wavelengths and the tweeter's short ones travelling at the same speed; the AP item on the orchestra tuning asks the student to expose the flaw in reading the wave equation as a dependence of speed on frequency.

concepts.name: Frequency stays fixed when sound changes medium
concepts.why: When sound travels from one medium to another its speed changes, but its frequency usually remains the same, because it is like a driven oscillation and has the frequency of the original source. Since the speed changes and the frequency does not, the wavelength must change: the higher the speed of sound, the greater the wavelength for a given frequency.
concepts.evidence: The paragraph after Example 17.1 states it; the second conceptual question asks whether frequency or wavelength changes at a boundary; the keyed problem on a dolphin's sound in air and in seawater computes the ratio of the two wavelengths.

concepts.name: Finding a distance from an echo's return time
concepts.why: A bat uses sound echoes to find its way about and to catch prey, and sonar and medical imaging use them the same way: the time for an echo to return is directly proportional to the distance, since the sound travels out and back at the speed of sound in the medium. The precision with which the echo time can be measured sets the smallest difference in distance that can be told apart.
concepts.evidence: Figure 17.9 shows the bat and its echo; the problems on the submarine's 1.20 s echo, the sonar with 0.0100 s precision, the fireworks lag of 0.400 s and the bat's insect at 3.00 m are each a distance from a time and a speed, and 17.7 uses the same reckoning for the depth of a tissue boundary.

concepts.name: Intensity of a sound wave, $\kIntens = \kP/A$
concepts.why: Intensity is the power per unit area carried by a wave, where power is the rate at which energy is transferred by the wave, and its SI unit is the watt per metre squared. It is the physical quantity behind the loudness we are all familiar with, and it is valid for every sound whether or not it is in the audible range. The intensities of ordinary sounds are quite small: only about 10⁻¹⁶ W falls on the eardrum at the threshold of hearing.
concepts.evidence: The definition opens the section and the summary; the paragraph on the eardrum's square centimetre turns it into a power; the problems on the eardrum exposed for eight hours, the ear trumpet, the stethoscope and the loudspeaker's power input each go between power, area and intensity.

concepts.name: Intensity and pressure amplitude, $\kIntens = (\kdpamp)^2/2\krho\kvw$
concepts.why: The intensity of a sound wave is related to its amplitude squared. The pressure amplitude is half the difference between the maximum and minimum pressure in the wave, the density is that of the material the sound travels in, and the speed is the speed of sound in that medium. The energy of an oscillating element of air is proportional to its amplitude squared, and the pressure variation is proportional to the amplitude of the oscillation, so the intensity goes as the square of the pressure amplitude: the greater the amplitude, the more the air is compressed in the sound it creates.
concepts.evidence: The equation follows the definition of intensity and is repeated in the summary; Figure 17.12 draws two gauge-pressure graphs of different amplitude; Example 17.2 computes the intensity of a 0.656 Pa wave; the keyed AP item on tripling an alarm's volume asks how many times the energy grows, and the problems on the 0.5 Pa wave, the 40.0 dB rise and the maximum gauge pressures at 60 and 120 dB turn on the square.

concepts.name: Sound intensity level in decibels, $\beta\ (\text{dB}) = 10\log_{10}(\kIntens/\kIo)$
concepts.why: Sound intensity levels are quoted in decibels much more often than intensities in watts per metre squared, because how our ears perceive sound is more accurately described by the logarithm of the intensity than by the intensity itself. The level of a sound of intensity $I$ is ten times the logarithm of its ratio to the reference intensity $I_0 = 10^{-12}$ W/m². Because it is defined in terms of a ratio it is a unitless quantity telling you the level of the sound relative to a fixed standard, and the decibel indicates that the ratio's logarithm is multiplied by ten.
concepts.evidence: The definition, Table 17.2 of familiar sounds from 0 to 160 dB, Example 17.2's 87 dB and the second Check Your Understanding on common sounds at 10, 50 and 100 dB; the problems on the 85.0 dB sound, the lawn mower, the earphones and the −8.00 dB sound go each way between $I$ and $\beta$, and 17.7's problems on ultrasound at 10⁵ W/m² and 2.00 × 10⁻² W/m² do the same.

concepts.name: The threshold of hearing and the range of intensities
concepts.why: The reference intensity $I_0 = 10^{-12}$ W/m² is the lowest intensity of sound a person with normal hearing can perceive at a frequency of 1000 Hz, and its level is 0 dB because the logarithm of one is zero. The ear is sensitive to as little as a trillionth of a watt per metre squared, when the air molecules vibrate over less than one molecular diameter and the gauge pressures are less than 10⁻⁹ atm, and it tolerates sounds 10¹² times as intense; a range that wide is why the logarithmic scale fits experience better than the intensities themselves.
concepts.evidence: The paragraphs after Table 17.2 make the two observations, on how small the intensities are and how wide their range is; the problems on 10⁻¹² W/m² as 10⁻¹⁶ W/cm² and on the 0 dB gauge pressure of 10⁻⁹ atm test the numbers, and 17.6's problems on measuring distances and speeds over a factor of 10¹² and 10³ test the range.

concepts.name: Ratios of intensities as differences in level, $\beta_2 - \beta_1 = 10\log_{10}(\kItwo/\kIone)$
concepts.why: Each factor of 10 in intensity corresponds to 10 dB, so a 90 dB sound is three factors of 10, or 1000 times, as intense as a 60 dB sound. Because the logarithm of a ratio is the difference of the logarithms, the difference in level between two sounds depends only on the ratio of their intensities: doubling the intensity raises the level by about 3 dB and a factor of five raises it by 7 dB, whatever the intensities themselves are.
concepts.evidence: Table 17.3 lists the ratios 2, 5 and 10 against 3.0, 7.0 and 10.0 dB; Example 17.3 shows that twice the intensity is 3.01 dB more; the conceptual question on the mayor's 30 dB and the problems on twice or one-fifth a 90.0 dB sound, 7.00 dB lower and 3.00 dB higher, and 17.0 dB and 23.0 dB apart are all this relation.

concepts.name: Adding the intensities of many sources
concepts.why: When many sources sound together and interference can be neglected, their intensities add, and the level rises by ten times the logarithm of how many there are: a thousand flies at 40.0 dB each make 70.0 dB, and ten stereos making 120 dB at the centre of a circle each contribute 110 dB. The rule is the decibel relation applied to a ratio that is a count.
concepts.evidence: The keyed problem on the housefly and its thousand companions, the problem on the ten cars at a boom box competition, and the Sim of many sources sounding together, which raises the level by ten times the logarithm of how many sources there are.

concepts.name: The sound pressure level
concepts.why: There is another decibel scale in use, the sound pressure level, based on the ratio of the pressure amplitude to a reference pressure rather than of intensity to a reference intensity. It is used particularly where sound travels in water, and very different decibel numbers can be quoted for the same sound: ocean noise from ships may be 200 dB as a sound pressure level where the sound intensity level would be under 140 dB, and 17.7 notes that its numbers run 60 to 70 dB above the levels this text uses.
concepts.evidence: The paragraph after Example 17.3 and its glossary entry; 17.7's paragraph on the 220 dB ultrasound and its conceptual question on the 210 dB figure that seems unreasonably high.

concepts.name: The Doppler effect
concepts.why: The Doppler effect is an alteration in the observed frequency of a sound due to motion of either the source or the observer, and the actual change in frequency is the Doppler shift. Each compression spreads out spherically from the point where it was emitted; when the source moves, the point of emission moves, so the compressions are closer together ahead of the source and farther apart behind it, and since the speed of sound in the medium is fixed, a shorter wavelength is received as a higher frequency. When the observer moves instead, the rate at which she meets the compressions changes. Relative motion toward one another raises the received frequency, motion apart lowers it, and the greater the relative speed, the greater the effect.
concepts.evidence: The motorcycle and the warning bell open the section; Figures 17.13, 17.14 and 17.15 draw the stationary source, the moving source and the moving observers; both Check Your Understanding boxes, the keyed AP item on the landing plane, the conceptual question on whether the shift is real and the boxed note on Doppler shifts in light and water waves.

concepts.name: Doppler shift for a moving source, $\kfobs = \kfsrc\left(\kvw/(\kvw \pm \kvs)\right)$
concepts.why: For a stationary observer and a moving source, the frequency received is the source frequency times the ratio of the speed of sound to the speed of sound plus or minus the source's speed along the line joining them, the minus sign for motion toward the observer and the plus sign for motion away. The greater the speed of the source, the greater the effect, and the shifts toward and away are not symmetric.
concepts.evidence: The equation and its sign rule; Example 17.4(a) finds 167 Hz and 136 Hz for a 150 Hz horn at 35.0 m/s; the problems on the ambulance, the jet at the air show, the hawk and the mouse, the trumpeter and the commuter train all use it, the last two solved for the speed.

concepts.name: Doppler shift for a moving observer, $\kfobs = \kfsrc\left((\kvw \pm \kvobs)/\kvw\right)$
concepts.why: For a stationary source and a moving observer, the frequency received is the source frequency times the ratio of the speed of sound plus or minus the observer's speed to the speed of sound, the plus sign for motion toward the source and the minus sign for motion away. The form differs from the moving-source case because the observer passes through more or fewer crests of a wave whose wavelength is unchanged.
concepts.evidence: The equation and its sign rule; the problem on pulling a tuning fork toward you at 10.0 m/s asks whether the shift can be perceived; 17.7's blood, as a moving observer, receives its first shift by this form.

concepts.name: Doppler shift when both source and observer move
concepts.why: When both move relative to the air there are two Doppler shifts, one for the moving observer and one for the moving source, and the received frequency is the product of the two factors. Source and observer carried together, as an engineer and the horn of the same train, receive the emitted frequency unchanged because the factors cancel; what matters is that they are not moving relative to each other.
concepts.evidence: Example 17.4(b) writes the bracketed product and shows everything but the source frequency cancelling; the keyed problem on the two eagles screeching at each other applies both factors; 17.7's Doppler-shifted ultrasound is the same double shift with the blood as reflector.

concepts.name: Sonic booms
concepts.why: As a source's speed approaches the speed of sound the observed frequency ahead of it approaches infinity, because each successive wave is superimposed on the previous one. If the source exceeds the speed of sound, no sound reaches an observer until the source has passed, and the waves interfere constructively along the lines of a cone: this superposition is a sonic boom, a constructive interference of sound created by an object moving faster than sound. Inside the cone the interference is mostly destructive. The faster the source, the smaller the cone's angle, and an aircraft makes two booms, one from its nose and one from its tail.
concepts.evidence: The Sonic Booms to Bow Wakes passage; Figures 17.16 and 17.17; the conceptual questions on why the plane cannot be seen and on the Mach number of a supersonic transport flying into colder air.

concepts.name: Bow wakes
concepts.why: Sonic booms are one example of a bow wake, the V-shaped disturbance created when a wave source moves faster than the wave propagation speed. Water waves spread in circles from the point where they are made, and a duck moving faster than they spread leaves the familiar wake; a subatomic particle moving through water faster than light moves in water leaves a cone of light called Cerenkov radiation.
concepts.evidence: Figure 17.18's duck and Figure 17.19's reactor pool; the paragraph on bow wakes and its glossary entry.

concepts.name: Sound interference
concepts.why: Interference is the hallmark of waves, and one way to prove something is a wave is to observe interference effects. Sound waves in fluids are pressure waves consistent with Pascal's principle, so pressures from two sources add and subtract like simple numbers: positive and negative gauge pressures add to a much smaller pressure and a lower-intensity sound. Noise-cancelling headphones introduce a second sound with its maxima and minima exactly reversed from the incoming noise, and the beats from two similar notes played together are interference too.
concepts.evidence: The opening paragraphs and Figure 17.21's headphones; the first Check Your Understanding; the AP items on two pulses passing through each other, their overlap, the amplitudes $A$ and $3A$, and the demonstration with two sound sources; the beat-frequency problems on the two horns, the notes A and C, the three piano strings and the piano tuner.

concepts.name: Resonance of an air column
concepts.why: An air column has only certain natural frequencies. A disturbance from a tuning fork travels down a tube at the speed of sound and bounces off the closed end; if the tube is just the right length the reflected sound arrives back at the fork exactly half a cycle later and interferes constructively with the continuing sound, and the incoming and reflected sounds form a standing wave. Only the resonant frequencies interfere constructively to form standing waves, while others interfere destructively and are absent, which is why every sound resonance, from a bottle's toot to a singer's voice, is a matter of interference. It is best considered a natural vibration of the air column independently of how it is induced.
concepts.evidence: Figures 17.22 to 17.25 follow the disturbance down the tube and back; Figure 17.26 drives the same standing wave from the closed end; the boxed note on resonance in everyday systems; the keyed AP items on which media standing waves form in and on the two tubes before one speaker.

concepts.name: Nodes and antinodes in a tube
concepts.why: The standing wave in a tube closed at one end has its maximum air displacement, an antinode, at the open end where motion is unconstrained, and no displacement, a node, at the closed end where air movement is halted. The distance from a node to an antinode is one-fourth of a wavelength, so for the lowest resonance the wavelength is four times the tube's length. A tube open at both ends has antinodes at both ends and half a wavelength inside for its lowest resonance.
concepts.evidence: The paragraph after Figure 17.25 defines both terms and derives $\lambda = 4L$; Figure 17.28 and Figure 17.30 mark the displacements along closed and open tubes; the second Check Your Understanding asks how a node and an antinode give the length of a closed tube.

concepts.name: Fundamental, overtones and harmonics
concepts.why: The lowest resonant frequency of a system is its fundamental, all higher resonant frequencies are overtones, and because every resonant frequency is an integral multiple of the fundamental they are collectively called harmonics: the fundamental is the first harmonic, the first overtone the second harmonic, and so on. For a tube closed at one end the first overtone is three times the fundamental and so is the third harmonic; which overtones are present and how intense they are is what makes a trumpet's middle C differ from a clarinet's and one voice from another.
concepts.evidence: The paragraph introducing the terms; Figure 17.28's fundamental and three overtones; the paragraph on the trumpet, the clarinet and the vowels of speech with Figure 17.29; the conceptual question on the difference between an overtone and a harmonic; the keyed AP item on the fourth overtone's frequency and wavelength.

concepts.name: Resonant frequencies of a tube closed at one end, $\kfn = n\kvw/4L$, $n = 1, 3, 5, \ldots$
concepts.why: With one-fourth of a wavelength in the tube at the fundamental and three-fourths at the first overtone, the pattern generalises to a single expression: the resonant frequencies of a tube closed at one end are odd multiples of the speed of sound over four times the length. They depend on the speed of sound and hence on temperature, which is why musicians bring their wind instruments to room temperature before playing them together.
concepts.evidence: The derivation from $\lambda = 4L$ through $f' = 3f$ to the general form, repeated in the summary; Example 17.5's 0.672 m tube with a 128 Hz fundamental and its fourth overtone at 1.15 kHz; the problems on the tuba's overtones, the organ pipe at 18.0 °C and 25.0 °C, the ear canal as a closed tube, the voice as a 0.240 m tube in air and in helium, the water-filled tube in the lab and the 1.80 m tube's audible frequencies; the keyed AP items on the glass half-full of water and on the length-against-frequency data.

concepts.name: Resonant frequencies of a tube open at both ends, $\kfn = n\kvw/2L$, $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$
concepts.why: A tube open at both ends has maximum air displacements at both ends, so its resonant frequencies are all integer multiples of the speed of sound over twice the length. Its fundamental is twice what it would be if the tube were closed at one end, and it has a different spectrum of overtones, which is why two tubes with the same fundamental, one open and one closed, sound different when played.
concepts.evidence: The equation, Figure 17.30 and the summary's second result; the conceptual question on which of two instruments of identical length can produce the lowest frequency; the keyed problems on the 0.672 m open tube, the bassoon's overtones and the oboe's length, and the problems on the flute for middle C and the tube with a 176 Hz fundamental and a 352 Hz first overtone.

concepts.name: Finding a tube's length or frequency from the speed of sound
concepts.why: To find the length of a tube that sounds a given fundamental, or the frequency a given length sounds, the speed of sound on the day is found first from the air temperature, and the resonance relation for the tube's kind of ends is then solved for the unknown. The same reckoning gives the range of fundamentals of the ear canal and the fraction by which an instrument's frequencies change between a cold and a warm room.
concepts.evidence: Example 17.5 finds the speed at 22.0 °C and then the length; the problems on the flute, the organ pipe, the ear canal between 1.80 and 2.60 cm, the voice tube, the lab's resonance tube and the 10.0 °C to 30.0 °C frequency ratio; the AP item on determining the speed of sound and the temperature of a cold classroom from standing waves.

concepts.name: Resonance in musical instruments
concepts.why: Wind instruments use resonance in air columns to amplify tones made by lips or reeds, and string instruments use sounding boxes: the vibrating string creates a sound that resonates in the box, greatly amplifying it and creating overtones that give the instrument its characteristic flavour, the more complex the box's shape the wider the range of frequencies it can resonate over. A marimba's gourds and a violin's body do the same work, and so does the cavity of the throat and mouth in speech. The ideas apply to any system with wave characteristics, down to the standing waves of an atom's electrons.
concepts.evidence: Figures 17.31 and 17.32 and their paragraph; the conceptual question on why an unamplified guitar is so much more intense than a string held taut by a stick; the closing paragraph on strings and atomic orbitals.

concepts.name: The audible range, infrasound and ultrasound
concepts.why: Normal human hearing encompasses frequencies from 20 to 20,000 Hz. Sounds below 20 Hz are infrasound and those above 20,000 Hz are ultrasound; neither is perceived by the ear, though infrasound can sometimes be felt as vibrations. Other animals hear differently: dogs to 30,000 Hz, bats and dolphins to 100,000 Hz, elephants below 20 Hz.
concepts.evidence: The second paragraph and the glossary's ultrasound and infrasound; the Check Your Understanding on whether ultrasound and infrasound are imperceptible to all hearing organisms; the problem on a speedometer spanning the same factor of 10³ as the ear's frequencies; 17.7 opens from the 20 kHz boundary.

concepts.name: How finely pitch is discriminated
concepts.why: Most of us have excellent relative pitch and can tell whether one sound has a different frequency from another when the frequencies differ by 0.3% or more, so that 500.0 and 501.5 Hz are noticeably different. Pitch perception is directly related to frequency and is not greatly affected by intensity. Musical notes are particular sounds with particular names, and the uncommon ability to name one on hearing it is perfect pitch.
concepts.evidence: The paragraph on pitch, relative pitch, notes and perfect pitch; the keyed problem on the closest frequencies to 500 Hz that can be told apart and the problem on 2002 Hz against 1999 Hz; 17.4's problems on the smallest perceptible Doppler shift use the same 0.300%.

concepts.name: Loudness and its dependence on frequency
concepts.why: The perception of intensity is loudness. At a given frequency a difference of about 1 dB can be discerned and a change of 3 dB is easily noticed, but loudness is not related to intensity alone: the ear has its maximum sensitivity between 2000 and 5000 Hz, so sounds there seem louder than sounds at 500 or 10,000 Hz of the same intensity, and sounds near the extremes of the hearing range seem less loud still. The ear responds over a range of a trillion in intensity, which very few instruments can match.
concepts.evidence: The paragraph defining loudness and Table 17.4 of perceptions against physical quantities; the keyed problems on the next clearly quieter level below 85 dB and on the ratio of intensities just discernible as louder, and the problem on the television going from 70 to 73 dB.

concepts.name: Timbre, tone and note
concepts.why: When a violin and a piano play the same middle C there is no mistaking one for the other, because each produces a distinctive set of frequencies and intensities. Our perception of these combinations is tone quality, or timbre, described by words such as dull, brilliant, warm or rich; it is more subjective than loudness or pitch and takes the subject into perceptual psychology. A note is the basic unit of music with a specific name, and combinations of notes constitute music.
concepts.evidence: The paragraph on the violin and the piano and Table 17.4's rows for timbre, note and tone; 17.5's account of overtone mixtures is the physics behind it.

concepts.name: Reading loudness in phons from the equal-loudness curves
concepts.why: A phon is the unit of loudness perception, as the decibel is the unit of physical intensity level, and the two are taken to be numerically equal at 1000 Hz. The equal-loudness curves relate loudness to intensity level and frequency for persons with normal hearing: any sound along a given curve is perceived as equally loud. To find a sound's loudness, locate its frequency and intensity level on the grid and interpolate between the curves; to find the level a sound needs for a given loudness, follow that curve to the frequency. The curves dip between 2000 and 5000 Hz, where the ear is most sensitive, and rise at both extremes; sounds below the 0-phon curve are not heard, and a few sounds below 0 dB are.
concepts.evidence: Figure 17.34; Example 17.6's three lookups at 100 Hz and 80 dB, 4000 Hz and 70 phons, and 200 Hz and 60 dB; the paragraph reading the graph's facts; the keyed problems on the threshold at 60, 400, 1000, 4000 and 15,000 Hz, the 600 Hz tone at 20 and 70 phons, and the just-audible 200 Hz and 4000 Hz intensities, and the problems on 40 phons at three frequencies and 60 phons at 60.0 and 10,000 Hz.

concepts.name: Hearing loss, the speech region and audiograms
concepts.why: Most conversational sound falls in a band of frequencies and intensity levels, and a hearing loss of 40 phons at all frequencies still allows conversation to be understood, though quietly, while a 60-phon loss leaves only the lowest frequencies and speech is not understood unless much louder than normal. Hearing tests run from 250 to 8000 Hz and are displayed as an audiogram, whose threshold is measured relative to the normal threshold so that normal hearing registers as 0 dB at every frequency. Loss caused by noise shows a dip near 4000 Hz whatever frequency caused it; the most common loss, presbycusis, comes with age and is increasingly severe at higher frequencies.
concepts.evidence: Figure 17.35's speech region with the 0-, 40- and 60-phon thresholds and Figure 17.36's three audiograms; the conceptual question on a 0 dB threshold at 250 Hz; the keyed problems on the 50 dB loss's factors of ten, the 10 dB and 50 dB thresholds at 100 and 4000 Hz, and the problems on the 5.0 × 10¹² amplification and the child's 60 dB loss near 5000 Hz.

concepts.name: The hearing mechanism
concepts.why: The ear is a transducer that converts sound waves into electrical nerve impulses. The outer ear, or ear canal, carries sound to the eardrum and resonates as an air column, which is partly why the ear is most sensitive between 2000 and 5000 Hz; the middle ear's lever system takes the force the sound pressure exerts on the eardrum, amplifies it and applies it through the oval window to the much smaller area of the cochlea, creating pressure waves about 40 times greater than those on the eardrum, while two muscles react to intense sound in a few milliseconds and reduce the force transmitted. In the inner ear the pressure waves make the tectorial membrane vibrate against the hair cells, which resonate at different positions for different frequencies, high near the base and low at the far end; below about 1000 Hz the nerves signal at the sound's own frequency, and above it by position. Conductive losses can be bypassed through the skull, and lost cilia can be replaced by a cochlear implant that stimulates the nerves directly.
concepts.evidence: The boxed note The Hearing Mechanism with Figure 17.37; Figure 17.38's lever and Figure 17.39's cochlea with their paragraphs; the paragraphs on hearing aids and the cochlear implant; 17.5's problems on the ear canal as a closed tube rest on the outer ear's resonance.

concepts.name: Ultrasound as a probe and as a treatment
concepts.why: Ultrasound is any sound above 20 kHz, and its characteristics, frequency, intensity and a wavelength that limits the detail it can detect, are wave properties common to all waves. Like any wave it carries energy that the medium absorbs, with effects that vary with intensity: focused to 10³ to 10⁵ W/m² it shatters gallstones and pulverises tissue, partly through cavitation, the creation and collapse of vapour cavities; at 10³ to 10⁴ W/m² it is the deep heating of ultrasound diathermy; diagnostic intensities of about 10⁻² W/m² are too low to do thermal damage, and decades of use show no ill effects.
concepts.evidence: The opening paragraphs and the note Characteristics of Ultrasound; the Ultrasound in Medical Therapy passage with Figure 17.41; the Check Your Understanding on why ultrasound can both image a fetus and destroy a tumour; the problems on the 170 dB, 155 dB and 103 dB levels of surgical, heating and diagnostic ultrasound; the conceptual question on the 210 dB figure.

concepts.name: Acoustic impedance, $Z = \krho\kv$
concepts.why: Reflections at boundaries between two media occur because of differences in their acoustic impedance, the product of a medium's density and the speed of sound through it, in kg/(m²·s). The acoustic impedances of soft tissues do not vary much, but there is a big difference between soft tissue and air and between soft tissue and bone, which is why those boundaries reflect so strongly.
concepts.evidence: The definition and Table 17.5 of densities, speeds and impedances; Example 17.7(a) verifies fat's 1.34 × 10⁶ kg/(m²·s); the keyed problem on the transducer coupled to air and to gel uses the table's values; and the Sim of a beam meeting a boundary, which draws the reflected and transmitted shares from the two impedances.

concepts.name: Intensity reflection coefficient, $a = (Z_2 - Z_1)^2/(Z_1 + Z_2)^2$
concepts.why: At a boundary between media of different acoustic impedance some of the wave energy is reflected and some transmitted, and the greater the difference in impedance the greater the reflection. The intensity reflection coefficient is the ratio of the reflected intensity to the incident intensity; it is zero, total transmission, when the two impedances are the same, and an impedance match is what couples sound efficiently from one medium into another. An ultrasound image is made by tracking these reflections and mapping their intensity in a plane.
concepts.evidence: The definition; Example 17.7(b) finds that only 1.4% of the intensity reflects between fat and muscle; the keyed problem on the transducer and air (1.00) against the transducer and gel (0.823) explains why gel is used; the conceptual question on imaging a heavier patient.

concepts.name: Resolution and penetration of an ultrasound probe
concepts.why: A transducer, a piezoelectric crystal, both sends the ultrasound and records its echoes, and the time between the signal and each echo gives the depth of each boundary at the speed of sound in tissue, about 1540 m/s. It is very difficult to detect details smaller than the wavelength of a probe: at 7 MHz the wavelength in tissue is 0.22 mm, and in practice 1 mm detail is attainable. Higher frequencies give finer detail but penetrate less, the rule of thumb being a useful depth of about 500 wavelengths, so they suit small organs such as the eye and not the deep abdomen.
concepts.evidence: Figure 17.42's echo graph and the Ultrasound in Medical Diagnostics passage with Figures 17.43 and 17.44; the paragraph on the wavelength limit and the 500λ rule; the problems on the 0.13 ms echo in fat, the 0.250 mm detail, the 20.0 MHz probe and the eye, the 3.50 and 3.60 cm echo times, the 0.750 μs difference, the bat's 1.00 ms echoes and the dolphin's two sharks; the conceptual question on which of a neighbour's frequencies penetrate.

concepts.name: Doppler-shifted ultrasound and its beat frequency, $\kfB = |\kfobs - \kfsrc|$
concepts.why: Ultrasound reflected from moving blood or a beating fetal heart is Doppler shifted twice: the reflector receives a shifted frequency as a moving observer and then returns it as a moving source, and the magnitude of the shift is directly proportional to the reflector's velocity. The echo is superimposed on the broadcast frequency to produce beats, and the beat frequency, the absolute difference of the two, is easy to measure where the shift itself, a few hundred hertz out of a couple of megahertz, is not, is unaffected by a drift in the broadcast frequency, and falls in the audible range. Doppler radar measures wind, aircraft and car speeds by the same principle.
concepts.evidence: The paragraph on Doppler-shifted ultrasound with Figure 17.45; Example 17.8's blood at 20.0 cm/s, its two shifts and the 649 Hz beat; the note on Doppler radar; the keyed problem on the 30.0 cm/s bloodstream's 974 Hz beat and the problem solving a 500 Hz shift for the blood's velocity.
